sources.title: Are You Ready? An In-Depth Guide to Citizen Preparedness (P-2064, September 2020)
sources.supports: Fetched the full 36-page text; read the contents list and the sections cited here (introduction, protective actions, financial preparedness, Make a Plan, supplies, documents, practice schedule). The hazard-by-hazard sections were not read. Three-step frame (know your risks, make a plan, take action); first moves when something happens without warning (assess the situation, decide to stay or change location); family communication plan with an out-of-state contact reachable two ways and a wallet or digital copy for everyone; evacuation guidelines (meeting places in several directions, half-tank rule, one car per family, leave a note); basic kit contents and the 'at least 72 hours' framing; water of 1 gallon per person per day for 3, 7 or even 14 days depending on location; cash in small bills with the highest a twenty; N95 respirators; kit maintenance (first in, first out; discard swollen, dented or corroded cans; check needs every six months); critical-document storage; practice schedule and one-year timeline.
sources.notes: September 2020 edition, hosted under a 2021-11 upload path. Older than the Ready.gov web pages, so where they differ the web pages are newer. Upgraded from a placeholder in register.json. The power-outage section says 'If the power is out for more than a day, discard any medication that should be refrigerated, unless the drug's label says otherwise' and uses a two-hour 40 F food rule; FEMA's December 2023 power-outage fact sheet is newer and differs.

sources.title: Make A Plan
sources.supports: Four steps: meet with your household (five questions: alerts, shelter, evacuation route, communication plan, kit); assess household needs (ages, responsibilities for assisting others, locations visited, dietary and medical needs, disabilities and access and functional needs, languages, cultural and religious considerations, pets or service animals, school-aged children); document the plan with the free fillable form; practice it. Family meeting place that is familiar and easy to find.

sources.title: Build A Kit
sources.supports: Basic disaster supplies kit list (water, several days of non-perishable food, radio including NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert, flashlight, first aid kit, batteries, whistle, dust mask, plastic sheeting and duct tape, towelettes and garbage bags, wrench or pliers, manual can opener, local maps, phone and charger with backup battery); additional items (hygiene, medications, eyeglasses, infant supplies, pet supplies, cash, documents, bedding, clothing and sturdy shoes, fire extinguisher, matches, mess kits, paper and pencil, activities); store items in airtight bags in one or two easy-to-carry containers; maintenance (cool dry place, replace expired items, 're-think your needs every year'); kit locations (home, work for at least 24 hours, car).
sources.notes: Says to re-think needs 'every year'; the 2020 Are You Ready guide and the CDC pages say every six months. See the cluster notes.

sources.title: Ready Emergency Supply List (PDF)
sources.supports: Two-page printable checklist linked from the Build A Kit page. Same basic items; says the list is only a starting point and recommends at least two kits: one full kit at home and smaller portable kits at work, in a vehicle or other places where you spend time.
sources.notes: The PDF carries no date; the 2024-05 comes from the upload path only.

sources.title: Food (emergency food supplies)
sources.supports: Store at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food; choose foods your family will eat; remember special dietary needs; example items (ready-to-eat canned goods and a can opener, bars, cereal, peanut butter, dried fruit, juices, non-perishable milk, high-energy and comfort foods, infant food); refrigerator holds cold about four hours unopened; discard perishables above 40 F for two hours or more; do not eat from swollen, dented or corroded cans; use ready-to-feed formula, and bottled or boiled water as a last resort if mixing.

sources.title: Evacuation
sources.supports: Know your risks, when and where to go, what to bring; build a go-bag so you do not scramble; everyone knows where the bag is and who is responsible; several destinations in different directions; a pet-friendly place because most public shelters allow only service animals; prepare a go-bag to carry on foot or public transport plus supplies for longer trips by car; keep a half tank at all times; one car per family; what to do before leaving; evacuation route may be on foot.

sources.title: Car Safety
sources.supports: Emergency kit for the car with automobile extras (jumper cables, flares or reflective triangle, ice scraper, car phone charger, blanket, map, cat litter or sand); keep the gas tank full for evacuation or power outages; do not drive through flooded areas.

sources.title: Power Outages
sources.supports: What an extended outage can disrupt; take an inventory of items that rely on electricity; talk to your medical provider about a power-outage plan for powered medical devices and refrigerated medicines; refrigerator keeps food cold about four hours, a full freezer about 48 hours; discard food at 40 F or above for two hours or more; discard refrigerated medicine if power is out more than a day unless the label says otherwise; generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors and at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; CO detectors with battery backup on every level; never heat a home with a gas stovetop or oven.
sources.notes: Web page read in full on 2026-10-29. Its medicine line ('discard refrigerated medication if power is out more than a day unless the label says otherwise') repeats the 2020 FEMA guide and is stricter than FEMA's newer December 2023 fact sheet (start-fema-power-sheet), which adds 'call your doctor or pharmacist' and 'only use the medicine until you have a new supply'. Its fridge/food rule is two hours above 40 F; the 2023 sheet says more than 4 hours. Both discrepancies are stated on the three-day-kit page.

sources.title: Emergency Alerts
sources.supports: Wireless Emergency Alerts (no subscription or charge, distinct sound and vibration, not affected by network congestion, some phones need the setting enabled, older phones may not be capable); Emergency Alert System on broadcast TV and radio; NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards broadcasting 24 hours a day; IPAWS; FEMA App with alerts for up to five locations and shelter finder; local alerting authorities decide what to send and FEMA does not review or approve alerts.

sources.title: Financial Preparedness
sources.supports: Gather financial, personal and medical records; consider an emergency savings account and keep a small amount of cash in small bills at home because ATMs and cards may not work; obtain property (homeowners or renters), health and life insurance; homeowners insurance does not typically cover flooding; store important documents in a safety deposit box, external drive or the cloud; household identification, financial and legal, medical, insurance and contact lists; direct deposit or Direct Express for federal benefits because disasters can disrupt mail; scam cautions.
sources.notes: Mentions the pandemic in a few lines; the page is otherwise generic.

sources.title: People with Disabilities
sources.supports: Support network and contact list; tell the network where supplies are and consider giving a trusted person a key; plan accessible transportation; voluntary local registries; know more than one dialysis or treatment facility; talk to your doctor about keeping electric medical equipment running and ask your power provider about priority restoration; medical alert tags; communication cards; kit tips by disability (deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision, speech disability, intellectual or developmental, mobility including a spare battery and a lightweight manual chair, Alzheimer's and dementia); several days' supply of prescription medicines; extreme-heat cautions; direct deposit.

sources.title: Older Adults
sources.supports: 'Take Control in 1, 2, 3' guide (assess needs, make a plan, engage your support network); at least one support-network member should have an extra key, know where supplies are and know how to use lifesaving equipment or give medicine; ask clinics that give routine treatments about their emergency plans and back-up providers; plan transportation if you need help evacuating; copies of Medicaid, Medicare and insurance cards; not all shelters accept pets; direct deposit or Direct Express.

sources.title: Ready Kids
sources.supports: Everyone in the family can help prepare; Ready Kids has sections for kids, teens, families and educators, games, and a family emergency planning collection. The landing page itself carries no instructions.
sources.notes: Landing page only. We did not read the sub-pages (kids/make-a-plan, kids/prepare-your-family).

sources.title: Low and No Cost Preparedness (graphics collection)
sources.supports: Graphic text (English version): look for deals at garage sales and thrift stores for camping gear, tools and cookware; have a family evacuation plan; use the free preparedness resources and the free emergency communication plan form; consider adding older clothing that still fits to the kit; sign up for local emergency alerts.
sources.notes: Text is read from the graphic captions on the collection page. The page the graphic points to (ready.gov/low-and-no-cost) was not fetched.

sources.title: Stay Connected (Prepare Your Health)
sources.supports: Emergency action plan with important phone numbers and at least two meeting places; microchip pets and keep registration current; have multiple ways to communicate, and text messages often go through when calls do not; plan for children, older adults and pets.

sources.title: Prescriptions (Prepare Your Health)
sources.supports: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about an emergency supply; keep a list of prescriptions with diagnosis, dosage, frequency, supply needs and allergies; nonprescription drugs; cooler and chemical ice packs for medicines that need chilling; some states have emergency prescription refill laws, so learn yours.
sources.notes: Gives no number of days for a medicine supply.

sources.title: Making an Emergency Plan (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
sources.supports: List of supplies for at least a week; arrange alerts; contact list of the people who support your health, with arrangements for them to check on you directly; several places to go if you evacuate; pictures in the plan if helpful; plan for service animals and assistive technology; backup manual chair; practice the plan, review and update it every year, and share it with the people who support you.

sources.title: Building an Emergency Kit (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
sources.supports: Batteries and portable chargers for adaptive equipment; communication aids; at least one week's supply of prescription medications and a cooler for refrigerated ones; medical supplies and health documents; extra mobility devices if obtainable; contact list in a watertight container; supplies for pets and service animals; check kits every six months.

sources.title: Sheltering and Evacuating (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
sources.supports: Keep health-needs information with you and wear medical alert tags; accessible transportation may not be available in an emergency, so contact paratransit or local government ahead of time; tell shelter workers your needs; shelters must be accessible under the ADA; shelters must allow service animals, and under the Fair Housing Amendments Act disaster shelters are required to allow emotional support animals.

sources.title: Emergency Kit Checklist: Pregnant Women, Infants, and Children
sources.supports: Essential items list; prescription medications of at least a two-week supply; check expiration dates and function every six months; extra water if pregnant or lactating; additions for pregnancy, for an infant (0-12 months) and for a young child (1-5 years) including ID tags, wristbands and memorized phone numbers; the pregnancy list includes emergency birth supplies and a plan with the health care provider.
sources.notes: Two-week medication supply differs from the one-week (CDC disability page), several-day (Ready.gov) and 30-day (Red Cross) figures.

sources.title: Emergency List for Families With Infants and Young Children
sources.supports: Kit contents by feeding method (breast milk, pump, formula); ready-to-feed formula is the safest formula option in an emergency; check the kit monthly so formula matches the baby's current needs; diaper bag contents; items marked with an asterisk are unsafe if they cannot be cleaned with safe water and soap; consider a camp stove and pot for boiling water. Lists 'Infant pain reliever with acetaminophen' with no dosing, age or weight guidance anywhere on the page. Starred items: breast milk storage bags or containers, breast pump and parts, manual pump, powdered formula and preparation materials, pacifiers, bulb syringe.
sources.notes: Whole page re-read on 2026-10-30 (about 16,500 characters, no truncation). The 'reviewed' date (2024-02-15) is earlier than the 'published' date (2024-05-15) on the page itself; reproduced as shown. The two-page PDF version of the checklist was not read.

sources.title: Older Adults Emergency Preparedness
sources.supports: Identify likely disasters and community plans; build a support network and meet with helpers; plan to stay home at least two weeks or evacuate; sign up for local registries if you need help evacuating; back-up plan for power-dependent medical devices and medicines that must stay cold; two ways out of every room; property or renter's insurance; keep at least 30 days of medications and extra assistive items; review, practice and refresh the plan, supplies and documents now and every six months.
sources.notes: The American Red Cross is a congressionally chartered nonprofit, not a regulator or government agency. The page shows no date. Fetched and read in full (main content) on 2026-10-29.

sources.title: Emergency Preparedness (older adults and people with disabilities)
sources.supports: About half of people 65 and older have two or more chronic health problems; at a minimum build a kit with medication, food, water, batteries or chargers, pet and service-animal supplies and shelter locations; ACL's Medical Information Card and Communication Assistance Card; build a support network for communication, transportation and essential care; Eldercare Locator 1-800-677-1116; Disability Information and Access Locator (DIAL); SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline 1-800-985-5990; HHS emPOWER data exists to help communities plan for people who rely on electricity-dependent equipment.
sources.notes: Page header carries a noindex robots tag. The 'Last modified' date is as printed on the page.

sources.title: Multifamily Disaster Preparedness Plan Template
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD Exchange)
sources.supports: Read the introduction, disclaimer, table of contents and first 12 of 79 pages. An optional planning template for owners of multifamily properties; covers resident protection and safety, building protection and business continuity; the table of contents lists resident handouts, an evacuation special assistance form and a go-bag checklist. Supports only the statement that such a template exists. Does not establish any legal duty of any landlord or any HUD requirement.
sources.notes: Pages 13-79 were NOT read. The template's own disclaimer says it is a model for owners to adapt, that not all recommendations apply to every building, and that opinions in it do not necessarily reflect HUD's official position. Do not use it as evidence of what any owner is legally required to do. The RAD requirement it mentions was not checked against current HUD rules.

sources.title: Assistance for Housing and Other Needs
sources.supports: FEMA help applies to presidentially declared disasters and primary residences; rent and lodging expense reimbursement for displaced households; Serious Needs payments for essentials such as food, water, baby formula and medication; accessibility repairs; you may qualify even if you have insurance, after filing a claim; eligibility conditions include citizenship or qualified-alien status and identity verification; apply at disasterassistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-3362 or at a Disaster Recovery Center.
sources.notes: Main page content read in full on 2026-10-30 (about 6,250 characters). The page calls its eligibility list 'general conditions'; it does not say whether conditions vary by declaration or change over time. We did not read the Individual Assistance Program and Policy Guide it links to.

sources.title: Protecting People Who Live or Work in High-Rises
sources.supports: Know the exits and fire-safety features of your building; practice your exit route; do not prop stairway or corridor doors open; do not use elevators during a fire; close stair doors behind you; call 911; not all tall buildings meet modern standards; a person who cannot use the stairs should call 911 and be prepared to shelter in place, possibly in a room with the door closed and a wet towel sealing the cracks, or wait on a clear stair landing for help.
sources.notes: Whole page re-read on 2026-10-30 via direct download. A blog post written for fire educators; the exit and shelter-in-place messages are about FIRE in tall buildings and say nothing about other hazards. Not the same page as the 'usfa-fire-escape' placeholder in register.json.

sources.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008, December 2023)
sources.supports: English two-page sheet (pages 1-2 of a 34-page file) read in full as extracted text: make a plan for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; talk to your doctor to plan for medical devices and medication storage; generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings such as windows, doors or garages; never use a gas stovetop, oven, grill or dryer to heat a home; CO and smoke alarms with battery backup; refrigerator keeps food cold about 4 hours, full freezer about 48 hours; throw away refrigerated food above 40 F for more than 4 hours; 'Replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more, unless the drug's label says otherwise. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medications that have been at room temperature. Only use the medicine until you have a new supply.'
sources.notes: Newer than the 2020 FEMA guide and the Ready.gov power-outages web page, which say to discard refrigerated medication after a day and use a two-hour food rule. Pages 3-34 of the file yielded no extractable text (likely translations as images) and were not read. Downloaded directly with curl and converted with pdftotext because Firecrawl had no credits.
